nameStory: Fire cherry gets its fiery name from its remarkable ability to quickly colonize areas after forest fires, sprouting vigorously from root systems that survive the flames. This resilient tree is also called pin cherry because of its small, delicate cherries that hang like tiny red pins from the branches.
description: Fire cherry is a fast-growing, short-lived tree that typically reaches 15-25 feet tall with a slender trunk and open, irregular crown. It's a pioneer species that quickly fills in disturbed areas, clearcuts, and forest openings with its light green foliage and clusters of small white flowers in spring. The tree produces tiny bright red cherries in summer that birds absolutely love, hence another common name: bird cherry.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with finely serrated edges that feel thin and delicate between your fingers. They're bright green and typically 2-4 inches long, turning yellow to reddish in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers appear in flat-topped clusters of 3-8 blooms in late spring. Each flower has 5 rounded petals and gives off a faint, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Tiny bright red cherries, about the size of a pea, that ripen in midsummer. They're quite sour and astringent to taste, with a large pit relative to the small amount of flesh.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, reddish-brown bark that feels almost silky to the touch when young. As the tree ages, the bark develops horizontal lines called lenticels that look like small dashes.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, fast-growing tree with an open, somewhat scraggly appearance. Often grows in dense thickets from root sprouts, creating colonies of similar-sized trees.

habitat: Fire cherry thrives in disturbed areas throughout New England, including recent clearcuts, burned areas, roadsides, and forest edges. It prefers well-drained, acidic soils and full to partial sunlight, often growing alongside other pioneer species like aspen, birch, and red maple. You'll commonly find it at elevations up to 3,000 feet in mountainous areas.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in May after the leaves emerge, creating a delicate display against the fresh green foliage. This is when the tree is most noticeable and easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Bright red cherries ripen in July and August, quickly attracting birds and wildlife. The thin leaves provide light, dappled shade beneath the tree.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange-red before dropping, and the tree becomes quite bare and sparse-looking. The smooth, reddish bark becomes more prominent.
seasonality.winter: Identified by its slender silhouette, smooth reddish bark with horizontal lenticels, and small reddish buds. The tree's scraggly, open branching pattern is distinctive.

funFact: Fire cherry can live dormant underground for decades as root systems, then suddenly spring to life after a disturbance, creating what appears to be an instant forest of young trees that are actually all connected and potentially much older than they look.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with chokecherry, but fire cherry has much narrower, more lance-shaped leaves compared to chokecherry's broader, oval leaves. Memory trick: fire cherry leaves are thin like flames, chokecherry leaves are wide like a choking collar.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bird cherry,' this name is also used for several other Prunus species, which can cause confusion among field guides. Fire cherry is specifically the North American Prunus pensylvanica, not the European bird cherry (Prunus padus).
compareHints: Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes. Unlike chokecherry, fire cherry's flowers and fruits are in smaller, flatter clusters, and the leaves are much more slender and pointed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
